theme: The man of lawlessness; stand firm; work while you wait
readingInstruction: Read 2 Thessalonians 1:1-3:18. This short letter was written soon after the first. Read it for its three movements: encouragement in persecution (chapter 1), correction about the day of the Lord (chapter 2), and instruction about idleness (chapter 3).
settingTheScene: A few months after the first letter, Paul learned that the Thessalonians were still suffering and had become confused about the day of the Lord. Someone had claimed, perhaps in a letter allegedly from Paul, that the day of the Lord had already come. Some stopped working, expecting Christ at any moment. Paul writes to comfort the persecuted, correct the misunderstanding, and tell the idle to work.
observation: “To grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels” (1:7).
“Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed” (2:3).
“And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (2:8).
“Because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth” (2:13).
“So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us” (2:15).
“But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one” (3:3).
“If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (3:10).
“As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good” (3:13).
interpretation:
In chapter 1, Paul thanks God for their growing faith and love and boasts of their steadfastness in persecution. Their suffering is “evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God.” God will repay with affliction those who afflict them and grant relief to the afflicted “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire.” Justice will be done. Paul prays that God would make them worthy of his calling, that the name of Jesus may be glorified in them.

Chapter 2 is among the most debated passages in the New Testament. Paul urges them not to be shaken by claims that the day of the Lord has come. “Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.” Something restrains him, and when the restrainer is removed, the lawless one will be revealed. The Lord Jesus will kill him “with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.” His coming will be by the activity of Satan with false signs and wonders, deceiving those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth. Interpreters differ on who the man of lawlessness is: a future individual Antichrist, an institution, a series of persecuting powers (such as Rome or later empires), or a spirit of rebellion embodied in many figures. The restrainer is also variously identified as the Roman Empire, government, the Holy Spirit, or the preaching of the gospel. The key point is clear: Christ will triumph, and believers should not be frightened.

Paul then returns to thanksgiving: “God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.” He urges them to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught. A prayer: “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.”

Chapter 3 asks for prayer that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, and that they may be delivered from wicked and evil people. “But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.” Then the discipline of idleness. Some were living in idleness, mere busybodies. Paul reminds them of his own example: they worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.” This does not apply to those unable to work, but to those unwilling. He commands them to work quietly and earn their own living. “As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.” The letter ends with a benediction of peace and grace, and Paul’s signature as a mark of authenticity.
connection: Daniel 7:25, 9:27, 11:36-37 stand behind the man of lawlessness. Matthew 24:15-28 and 1 John 2:18-22 speak of antichrists. Revelation 13 and 19:19-21 describe the beast and Christ’s victory. Isaiah 11:4 speaks of slaying the wicked with the breath of his lips. 1 Thessalonians 4:11 and 5:14 also address idleness. Ephesians 4:28 and Proverbs 6:6-11 speak of work. Galatians 6:9 repeats the encouragement not to grow weary. John 17:15 prays that God would keep us from the evil one.
application:
If you are suffering for your faith or for doing right, take comfort in 1:5-7. God sees.

Ask if you are tempted to idleness or to being a busybody. What is one productive thing you can do today?

Memorize 3:3 as a promise: the Lord is faithful; he will establish and guard you.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he will be revealed from heaven and bring justice.
Ask him to help you stand firm and not be shaken.
Ask him to give you strength to keep working while you wait.
